name: Sara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a campaign manager at Northline, an outdoor clothing brand, mostly rain jackets and walking boots. I lead a little team of three inside the wider marketing group, so my day is planning launches, writing the big campaign lines myself and checking everyone else's. Today it was the spring jacket launch, and a two-hour argument about whether a puddle photo looks fun or just wet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy turning a dull product fact, like taped seams, into a story about a kid splashing on the way to school. What drains me is reporting: spreadsheets of clicks every Monday for people who never read them. I use an AI tool now and then for email subject lines, but I don't trust it with anything that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold, and that people panicked over a fancy autocomplete. At work I'd make a joke about all the training sessions we sat through for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means not much changes for me, and I'm fine with that. The Monday reports might get faster, which would be lovely. My job is the judgement calls, and those stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the team the way I do. I'd use the subject-line tool a bit more, and maybe let it draft the Monday report so I get two hours back. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit relieved for the younger people on my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work or money that worries you even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work or money that worries you even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the two hours you got back on Mondays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the two hours I got back on Mondays in the shop on the high street, talking to the people who actually buy the jackets. That's where the best campaign ideas always come from anyway. Software can't stand by the boot wall and listen.

say: I'd say AI was a **decent tool** that got oversold.
I'd joke about all the **training sessions** we sat through for nothing.
think: Not much changes for me, and the **judgement calls** stay mine.
The **Monday reports** would get faster, which I'd welcome.
do: Use the **subject-line tool** a little more for routine emails.
Let AI draft the **Monday report** to win back two hours.
Spend those hours **in the shop** listening to customers.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **relieved** for the younger people on my team.
S0.quote: Software can't stand by the boot wall and listen.
fieldNote: Sara is secure here: **steady household** income and a good year at Northline.
She treats AI as a **time-saver** for reports, not a threat.
Her instinct is to spend saved time **with customers**, which says a lot about her craft.

steps.text: Keep running the jacket campaigns with the same team of three
Let an AI tool draft the Monday clicks report

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on this, and a say for staff in how the tools are brought in. Online I'd share examples of companies doing it fairly, because I think it's possible. At work I'd ask HR straight out what the plan is for our roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my team of three probably becomes one plus software, and I'm likely the one. That's grim, because I'd be keeping my job by watching two people I hired lose theirs. Writing and planning are my whole day, so the change hits me now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the company's AI course seriously this time and get good at checking the tool's work, because that's the bit they'll still pay for. I'd push for a staff council at Northline so we're consulted before cuts. And I'd move an extra 200 a month into savings, to get from three months towards six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding into anxious. I'd feel like I was surviving by being the last one standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably be kept. Is that confidence or hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's half and half. I'm good, and I know the brand better than anyone, but a team of one is easy to fold into another department. Being kept now doesn't mean being kept in three years.

say: I'd say we need **rules**, and staff should get a **say** in the tools.
I'd ask HR directly what the **plan** is for our roles.
think: My team of three probably becomes **one plus software**.
I'd likely be kept while **two people I hired** lose their jobs.
Being kept now doesn't mean being **kept in three years**.
do: Take Northline's **AI course** seriously and learn to check the tool's work.
Push for a **staff council** to be consulted before cuts.
Save an **extra 200** a month to reach six months' cushion.
feel: Uneasy sliding into **anxious**, like **surviving** by being last one standing.
S1.quote: I'd be keeping my job by watching two people I hired lose theirs.
fieldNote: Sara's guilt about her **team** weighs as much as her own income.
She is **steady**: she'd learn the tools once Northline makes them official.
She openly doubts her own role survives beyond **three years**.

steps.text: Finish Northline's AI course and learn to check the tool's copy
Push for a staff council to be consulted before any cuts
Move an extra 200 a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer, fast: a guaranteed income, and the companies building it paying their share. I'd go to the protests, and I'd say it at work too. You can't ask people to adapt in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose my job, maybe within a year of it arriving. Everything I do is thinking work, and AGI is described as doing that better and cheaper. Jonas would still be driving for a few years until the robots come, so we'd be living on one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for work that's mostly face-to-face, like the climate group's community organising or a job in the Northline shop, since being in a room with people lasts longer. We'd cut the car, the holidays and eating out in the first month. And I'd go to every meeting pushing for a basic income, because I don't see another way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like the floor's moving and I'm the only one who's noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas talk about the first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas talk about the first night?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that gives you hope in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that everyone would be in it at once. If it's everybody, governments can't pretend it's our fault for not trying hard enough. That's a strange kind of hope, but it's real.

say: I'd call for a **guaranteed income** paid for by the companies building AGI.
I'd say you can't ask people to **adapt in two years**.
think: I'd likely **lose my job** within a year of AGI arriving.
We'd live on **one wage**, Jonas's, until driverless buses around 2031.
do: Look for **face-to-face** work like community organising or the Northline shop.
Cut the **car**, holidays and eating out in the first month.
Go to every meeting pushing for a **basic income**.
feel: **Scared**, like the floor is moving and I'm the only one noticing.
S2.quote: Jonas (her partner) drives a bus, so we'd be two people in a flat with three years on the clock.
fieldNote: Sara reasons through the **3-year gap**: her desk job goes first, Jonas's bus later.
Her hope is **political**: shared losses force governments to act.
She looks to **people-facing work** as the longest-lasting option.

steps.text: Apply for community organising work with the local climate group
Sell the car and cancel holidays in the first month
Campaign at local meetings for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is exactly the window to set up retraining and income support, and we're wasting it. I'd write to our local representative. At work I'd ask Northline to publish a transition plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three good years at Northline, then it's over for desk marketing. Five years means I can move before I'm pushed. I'd be 32, which is fine for starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time social work course in the first year, because it's people, judgement and visits, not screens. I'd keep using the AI tools at work to stay useful while I study. And we'd keep saving, aiming for six months by the time AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's the difference between falling and climbing down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why social work, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why social work, of all things?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Social work has paperwork too. Doesn't that get automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork would go, sure, and honestly good riddance. What's left is the visit itself, and for at least those three years after AGI nobody has a robot that can do it. I'd rather be doing the part that's left than the part that's gone.

say: I'd say five years is the window for **retraining** and support, and we're wasting it.
I'd ask Northline to publish a **transition plan**.
think: I'd get about **three good years** at Northline, then desk marketing ends.
At **32**, starting again is fine if I move before I'm pushed.
do: Start a part-time **social work** course in the first year.
Keep using **AI tools** at work to stay useful while I study.
Build savings to **six months** before AGI lands.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan, like **climbing down** instead of falling.
S3.quote: With five years, it's the difference between falling and climbing down.
fieldNote: The extra time lets Sara plan a **deliberate switch** to social work.
Her mum's career gives her a **model** for people-facing work.
She notes the **paperwork** goes but the home visit lasts longer.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time social work degree next September
Use Northline's AI tools daily to stay useful while studying
Save until the cushion reaches six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, if governments start now. I'd be loud about it being a choice whether this goes well or badly. At work I'd be fairly relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I can probably finish my career stage at Northline, maybe even become head of marketing. I'd be 37 when AGI lands. That's young enough to change, old enough to have savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work and learn the tools as they're proven. I'd start the social work idea slowly, maybe volunteering at weekends first to see if I like it. And I'd stay involved in campaigning for a fair transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It feels far enough away to think straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still tell young people to go into marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young people to go into marketing only if they love talking to customers more than writing. The writing part is borrowed time. The listening part might not be.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if governments start now.
I'd insist it's a **choice** whether this goes well or badly.
think: I could finish this stage at Northline, maybe become **head of marketing**.
At **37** I'd be young enough to change and have savings.
do: Keep working and learn **AI tools** as they're proven.
Try **weekend volunteering** in social care before committing to retrain.
Stay active campaigning for a **fair transition**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but far enough away to **think straight**.
S4.quote: I'd tell young people to go into marketing only if they love talking to customers more than writing.
fieldNote: Ten years makes Sara's job feel **safe for now**, so the mood eases.
She'd still buy a **small flat** sized to one wage, a quiet hedge.
Her advice to the young shows she sees **writing** as the part that goes.

steps.text: Keep leading Northline's jacket campaigns and aim for head of marketing
Volunteer at weekends with a local social care charity
Campaign for a fair transition with the climate group
Buy a small flat that one wage could cover

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to climb down, you just fall. What would help is a guaranteed income during the switch and free retraining for people-facing work like care and social work. Paid for by the people making the money from it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the manager in these stories. Everyone asks about the people cut, rightly. But somebody has to tell them, and in most of these pictures that somebody is me.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about the people cut, rightly, but in most of these pictures the person who has to tell them is me.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** campaign manager at Northline, an outdoor clothing brand, leading three people.
She is **progressive** and practical, wanting rules, staff councils and a guaranteed income.
She lives with Jonas, a **bus driver**, so the 3-year robot gap matters at home.
She's **steady**: she uses AI tools once proven and plans moves step by step.
Her escape route is **social work**, following her mum, and it firms up as time allows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's **no time** to climb down, you just fall.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** during the switch and **free retraining** for people-facing work.
